title: QBR KPI inference-to-business-metrics mapping playbook
author: Nina Park
summary: How to translate Redwood inference telemetry and model signals into customer business KPIs for QBRs. Includes a repeatable mapping matrix, telemetry queries, slide checklist, and escalation points to keep QBR conversations actionable.
body:
Overview

This playbook describes a repeatable process for mapping low-level inference telemetry (latency, p50/p95/p99, token usage, model variant switches, error rates, and cost-per-1000-tokens) to customer-facing business KPIs (conversion, time-to-answer, cost per active user, SLA adherence). The goal is to produce concise, business-oriented QBR slides that clearly identify risks, opportunities, and recommended actions.

When to use

- Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with product/ops stakeholders.
- Post-cutover stabilization reviews (weeks 1–6).
- Any time a model rollout or pricing change materially affects customer costs or latency.

Audience

- Customer success leads (owner)
- Customer engineering / integration contacts
- Internal product and platform stakeholders

Roles and responsibilities

1. Customer Success (CS) owner: assemble data, narrative, and slides; own action items.
2. Observability engineer: provide verified telemetry queries and raw data extracts.
3. Solutions engineer: validate mapping assumptions with customer integration details.
4. Finance/RevOps (if cost material): validate cost-per-unit computations.

Mapping matrix (example)

Use this matrix to convert telemetry signals into one-line business impacts. Replace values with customer-specific thresholds during prep.

| Inference telemetry signal | Typical threshold | Business KPI impacted | One-line interpretation for customer |
|---------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------------------------|
| p95 latency (in ms) | > 1200 ms | Time-to-answer / conversion | Increased answer time — potential drop in conversions for interactive flows |
| Token churn per session | +20% vs baseline | Cost per active user | Higher token usage → higher monthly bill per seat |
| Model fallback rate (%) | > 3% | Feature availability / SLA | Frequent fallbacks to cheaper variant → degraded feature fidelity |
| Streaming disconnects per 10k sessions | > 5 | User experience (dropouts) | Session truncation risk; affects retention during long sessions |
| Error rate (5xx) | > 0.5% | SLA and incident risk | Elevated errors → SLA may be breached; remediation required |
| Embedding latency (p99) | > 300 ms | Search relevance and UX | Indexing/search slowdown → query throughput/latency regressions |

Step-by-step prep for the QBR (2-week cadence before meeting)

1. Week -2: CS owner requests telemetry dumps from observability team for the past 90 days and a delta window of last 14 days. Define baseline period (customer’s historical median).
2. Week -2: Solutions engineer confirms model variants and expected tokenization differences for known flows. Document any recent prompt or prompt-template changes.
3. Week -10 days: Observability engineer runs production queries (examples below) and validates sampling. Attach raw CSVs to the QBR folder.
4. Week -7 days: CS owner drafts 6-slide narrative: headline, current-state metrics (business KPI), top 3 technical signals, root cause hypotheses, proposed actions, and ask.
5. Week -4 days: Circulate draft to reviewers (product, finance, customer-eng).
6. Week -1 day: Finalize slides and run internal dry-run with internal stakeholders.

Queries and telemetry snippets (examples)

Note: adapt to your telemetry stack (Prometheus, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Datadog). Below are pseudocode/SQL patterns.

- P95 latency (per route):
  SELECT route, PERCENTILE(latency_ms, 95) as p95_latency, date
  FROM inference_latency
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>' AND date >= DATE_SUB(current_date, INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  GROUP BY route, date

- Token churn per session (session-level token delta):
  SELECT session_id, SUM(output_tokens + input_tokens) as tokens, date
  FROM token_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY session_id, date

- Model fallback rate:
  SELECT date, SUM(fallbacks)/SUM(requests) as fallback_rate
  FROM request_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY date

Sample business narratives (write these as slide headlines)

- Headline (Good): "Stable inference latency; conversion unchanged; opportunities to reduce token churn by 12% via prompt templates."
- Headline (Risk): "p95 latency increased 45% in last 14 days — predicted 2–4% drop in trial-to-conversion for interactive chat flows."
- Headline (Cost): "Token churn up 30% after model upgrade: estimated $12k/mo incremental spend; recommended stop-gap: roll back or enable aggressive prefix caching."

Slide checklist for QBR

- One-line executive summary (impact + ask)
- Top-level business KPI(s) with trend lines (90d and 14d)
- Top 3 technical signals mapped to KPIs (with thresholds annotated)
- Root-cause hypotheses with confidence levels and data references
- Action plan with owners, ETA, and expected KPI delta (e.g., reduce p95 by 200 ms → recover 1.5% conversions)
- Financial impact estimate (if > $5k / month)
- Risk and rollback criteria for any recommended changes

Post-QBR follow-up and measurement

1. Create a triage ticket in CS board with: summary, telemetry links, owners, and success criteria.
2. Tag the ticket with labels: qbr-action, telemetry, cost-impact.
3. Observability engineer adds a synthetic test to the customer’s synthetic suite to verify the remediation.
4. Re-check the mapped KPIs at 7 and 30 days; report back as a short one-slide update.

Escalation thresholds (customer-facing)

- Immediate (page): p95 latency > 2x target and > 2 seconds for core interactive route.
- High (email & Slack CC): fallback rate > 10% sustained for 1 hour and impacting top route.
- Medium (ticket + weekly sync): token cost delta > 25% month-over-month and projected spend > $5k.

Operational tips and guardrails

- Use model variant tags in telemetry to attribute cost/quality to each variant.
- Normalize token cost calculations by customer-specific pricing tiers and reserved commit adjustments.
- Avoid attributing conversion regressions to model performance unless you can show temporal alignment and user cohort parity.

Appendix: sample mapping CSV (columns to include)

- timestamp, route, model_variant, requests, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, errors_5xx, tokens_in, tokens_out, fallbacks, synthetic_check_pass, notes
